reasoning.notes: Most non-forced decisions weigh the options against the state. Players infer voids from discards, count unseen cards, apply the Clubs tie-break relative to their own seat, and time Spades conversions to come before a Clubs theft, which is exactly what the designer listed. Many plays are routine follows of the lowest card, though, and a few contain miscounts.

evidence.quote: Playing a Spade off-suit moves that crystal into my vault first. That doubles its value and leaves nothing to steal.
evidence.shows: Times a Spades conversion just before the trick winner's Clubs theft.

evidence.quote: If I play a club off-suit now, I take that showroom crystal from them. I gain 1 point, and their Spades action then has nothing to move, so they lose 2. That is a 3-point swing against the leader.
evidence.shows: Uses action order within the trick to deny the leader's conversion, and counts the full swing.

evidence.quote: On a tie, seat 2 takes from the first seat clockwise after them, which is me.
evidence.shows: Applies the relative tie-break correctly and moves the theft onto the other opponent.

evidence.quote: Seat 3 has shown it holds no Hearts and no Clubs, so its last two cards are Spades or Diamonds.
evidence.shows: Infers an opponent's remaining hand from earlier discards and picks the lower-risk lead.

planning.notes: Players often void a suit with the pass and then use that void later, keep top cards to convert crystals later, and pursue the zero-trick bonus across a whole hand by shedding winners ahead of time. These plans are mostly within one hand, and few depend on predicting what opponents will do several tricks ahead.

evidence.quote: passing it leaves me with no hearts. Whenever hearts are led, I can then throw a low diamond (D1 or D3)
evidence.shows: Passes to create a void; this paid off with the D3 discard on trick 2.

evidence.quote: The plan is to win a Hearts trick first to put a crystal in my showroom. Then I lead S8, the top spade and a sure winner, to move that crystal into my vault.
evidence.shows: Sequences tricks over two turns so the Hearts gain is then converted by Spades.

evidence.quote: I'll play low, keep S8, and try to discard it the next time I can't follow suit, such as on a club lead.
evidence.shows: Sets up a later shed of a winner to keep the zero-trick bonus; carried out at turn 34.

evidence.quote: seat 1 should then take the Clubs bonus, and it would come out of seat 2's showroom rather than mine.
evidence.shows: Plans through the end-of-hand majorities, including where an opponent's bonus will land.

luck.notes: With only 21 of 32 cards in play and rank alone deciding tricks, holding the 8s or a hand of all low cards largely sets who wins tricks and who can chase the zero-trick bonus. Choices still moved several points through discards, conversions and thefts.

evidence.quote: My hand is all low cards, so going for zero tricks looks good
evidence.shows: The deal set the strategy; this seat went on to collect two zero-trick bonuses and win.

evidence.quote: C8 is the highest club, so leading it should win the trick.
evidence.shows: Sure tricks come from simply being dealt the top card.

weak_spots.what: Miscounted the hearts: it called H7 gone, but H7 was played in hand 2, not this hand. It then contradicted itself by saying only H7 could beat H6, and gave a made-up 73% figure. Tracking only the current hand's played cards would have given the correct odds.

Discarded S5 to keep S6–S8 for the spade majority, then switched to a zero-trick plan at turn 52 and was left with S6/S7, which won the trick on S1 anyway. Shedding the high spades first, while keeping the low ones to duck with, was the consistent plan once the showroom was empty.

Led C4 while holding the only crystal exposed to a Clubs theft, even though seat 1 had shown strength. Seat 1 won with C6 and took seat 2's crystal. H2 risked only a +1 Hearts gain for the trick winner instead of a 2-point swing.

summary: Winning rewards real reasoning about voids, action order within a trick and Clubs targeting, plus within-hand plans such as voiding a suit or chasing zero tricks, but who holds the top cards often decides who wins tricks. More information to plan around, such as revealing some of the 11 set-aside cards or giving a bigger reward for suit majorities, would make card counting and multi-trick planning matter more than the deal.
